# "I Can't Get Started": A Jazz Standard and Its Interpreters

"I Can't Get Started" stands as one of the most enduring songs of the American jazz repertoire, closely associated with trumpeter Bunny Berigan. Berigan first recorded the tune in 1936 with a small group, but it was his 1937 re-recording in a big-band setting that transformed the song into his signature piece, forever linking his name to the composition.

The song itself was the work of two celebrated craftsmen: lyricist Ira Gershwin and composer Vernon Duke. It made its Broadway debut in 1936 as a duet, introduced to audiences by Bob Hope and Eve Arden in *The Ziegfeld Follies*. From these theatrical origins, the song quickly found new life in the hands of jazz musicians.

Among the notable interpreters was Billie Holiday, who recorded her own acclaimed version within months of Berigan's landmark 1937 recording. Holiday's rendition was distinguished by exceptional accompaniment, backed by the tenor saxophonist Lester Young and the Count Basie Orchestra. Another singer connected to the song was Lee Wiley, who was romantically involved with Berigan and had appeared alongside him on CBS radio in 1936. Despite this personal connection to the trumpeter and the tune, Wiley recorded the ballad only once, and even then only informally, during a 1945 Town Hall performance.

The song's lyrics also carry a fascinating historical resonance. Gershwin's words reference the settling of "revolutions in Spain," a line that coincided with the Spanish Civil War. That conflict, which raged from 1936 to 1939, ultimately concluded with Franco's forces entering Madrid, lending the seemingly lighthearted lyric an unexpected connection to the turbulent world events of its era.
